To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

copper deficiency triggers coordinated genetic changes in the expression and accumulation of proteins and metabolites in the chloroplast, which are essential for maintaining photosynthesis in this condition.
copper deficiency induces changes in the accumulation of proteins involved in chlorophyl biosynthesis, and also in the expression and accumulation of proteins involved tocopherol biosynthesis.

(a) the expression of genes for enzymes in the chlorophyll biosynthetic pathway is copper-dependent and that this regulation is mediated by the transcription factor CGL78, which is itself copper-dependent; (b) the expression of the gene encoding 4-hypdroxyphenylpyrvate dioxygenase is copper-dependent and this regulation is mediated through CRR1, which itself is copper-dependent; and (c) copper deficiency triggers the accumulation of a chlorophyl-binding protein
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the genetic and biochemical consequences of copper deficiency on photosynthesis in Chlamydomonad algae.
the identification of genes involved in the response to environmental stresses.
the genetic and biochemical basis of changes in the expression and accumulation of key enzymes involved in lipid and pigment biosynthesis in response to copper-deficiency.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in the absence of copper, chlorophyll biosynthetic enzymes are down-regulated, while those involved in tocopherol and plastoquinone biosynthesis are up-regulated.

copper deficiency in Chlamydomonasshows that the expression of genes for chlorophyll, tocopherol, and plastochromanol biosyntheses is coordinated and that the resulting metabolites are important for protection against oxidative stress.

copper deficiency induces changes in the expression and/or activity of enzymes in the chloroplast-localized pathways of lipid and pigment biosyntheses that lead to increased abundance of the antioxidant metabolites γ-tocopherol, plastochromon-8 and LHCSR3, and that the latter may have a role in the protection against photo-oxidative damage.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

copper deficiency triggers a coordinated response that is genetically programmed to increase the abundance of antioxidants, which are required to counteract the effects of reactive oxygen species (ROS) that are generated by photosynthesis under conditions of reduced copper availability.

copper deficiency triggers a genetic program that results in the coordinated changes in the expression and abundance of proteins involved in chlorophyl biosynthesis, light harvesting, and antioxidant metabolism.

copper deficiency in C. reinhardtii triggers a coordinated set of changes in the expression and accumulation of proteins involved in chlorophyl, plastoquinone, and tocopherol metabolism, which may be important for the adaptation to this condition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, as in higher plants, copper deficiency in Chlamydomonassimulates the expression of genes involved in lipid/pigment metabolism, which in turn, may contribute to increased tolerance to this stress.

the copper-nutritional control of chlorophyll biosynthetic enzymes is a mechanism that can be used by cells to regulate the accumulation of other proteins and metabolites, including those with antioxidant functions.

the expression of genes in the lipid and pigment biosynthetic pathways is coordinated to provide the necessary cofactors for the photosynthetic apparatus, and that this is genetically programmed in response to environmental changes.
